stimulus.title: The Brass Lantern at Point Nepean
stimulus.body: Every afternoon at four o'clock, when the westerly wind began to rattle the tea-tree scrub along the headland, twelve-year-old Callum climbed the narrow iron staircase to the old lookout room. His grandfather had been the last keeper before the automated beacon replaced the oil lamps, and though the limestone tower no longer guided ships through the Rip, Callum treated the brass lantern as though it were still on duty. He wiped salt haze from the curved glass panes with a linen cloth and checked the logbook that remained open on the cedar desk. Inside, his grandfather's neat copperplate entries recorded wind speeds, passing barques, and the occasional pod of southern right whales sheltering in the bay. Callum's favourite entry, dated 14 July 1968, described a winter squall so fierce that spray reached the lantern gallery thirty metres above the tide. Beneath the date, his grandfather had written a single reminder: 'A steady light does not argue with the storm; it simply refuses to go out.' As dusk settled and the automated LED flashed twice a minute from the steel mast beside the tower, Callum closed the logbook, turned the brass latch, and descended into the salt-scented twilight.

workedSolution: The passage states Callum's grandfather was 'the last keeper before the automated beacon replaced the oil lamps.'
Exam technique: verify 'An automated beacon replaced the oil lamps.' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: Architects of the Mallee: The Mound-Building Malleefowl
stimulus.body: Unlike almost every other bird on Earth, the Australian malleefowl does not sit upon its eggs to keep them warm. Instead, this shy, ground-dwelling bird constructs an extraordinary natural incubator from sand, fallen eucalyptus leaves and twigs. Beginning in late autumn, a pair of malleefowl excavates a wide pit in the sandy soil of the mallee scrub and fills it with up to a tonne of leaf litter. When winter rains soak the buried vegetation, microbes begin to decompose the damp leaves, releasing steady warmth from below—much like a backyard compost heap. Once the mound reaches the right temperature, the female lays a clutch of eggs deep inside the chamber, and the male becomes a tireless thermal engineer. Every morning, he thrusts his sensitive beak into the sand to measure the internal heat. If the core rises above thirty-four degrees Celsius, he scrapes away layers of insulating sand to let excess heat escape; if a cold snap chills the mound, he piles fresh sand back on top or opens the crater at midday to capture solar warmth. Because newly hatched chicks must dig their way upward through nearly a metre of sand unaided, they emerge fully feathered and capable of running within hours—and flying within a single day.

Exam technique: verify 'Microbes decomposing the damp, buried leaf litter' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.

stimulus.body: Unlike almost every other bird on Earth, the Australian malleefowl does not sit upon its eggs to keep them warm. Instead, this shy, ground-dwelling bird constructs an extraordinary natural incubator from sand, fallen eucalyptus leaves and twigs. Beginning in late autumn, a pair of malleefowl excavates a wide pit in the sandy soil of the mallee scrub and fills it with up to a tonne of leaf litter. When winter rains soak the buried vegetation, microbes begin to decompose the damp leaves, releasing steady warmth from below—much like a backyard compost heap. Once the mound reaches the right temperature, the female lays a clutch of eggs deep inside the chamber, and the male becomes a tireless thermal engineer. Every morning, he thrusts his sensitive beak into the sand to measure the internal heat. If the core rises above thirty-four degrees Celsius, he scrapes away layers of insulating sand to let excess heat escape; if a cold snap chills the mound, he piles fresh sand back on top or opens the crater at midday to capture solar warmth. Because newly hatched chicks must dig their way upward through nearly a metre of sand unaided, they emerge fully feathered and capable of running within hours—and flying within a single day.
